title: Cross-Database SQL Compatibility
subtopics: Testing SQL against the intended database engine
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of cross-database sql compatibility.
Apply standard sql vs. dialect extensions in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn cross-database sql compatibility through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Cross-Database SQL Compatibility matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Cross-Database SQL Compatibility extends core SQL into a specialized area. Treat the engine and version as part of the example, verify the feature's availability, and keep an explicit fallback or note when an extension is required.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Standard SQL vs. dialect extensions, Date and time syntax differences, String and mathematical function differences, Row-limiting syntax. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Standard SQL vs. dialect extensions
items.text: Standard SQL vs. dialect extensions helps you explore optional advanced SQL including specialized types, JSON, full-text and spatial search, hierarchical data, temporal history, and portability decisions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Date and time syntax differences
items.text: Date and time syntax differences needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: String and mathematical function differences
items.text: String and mathematical function differences depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Row-limiting syntax
items.text: Row-limiting syntax helps you explore optional advanced SQL including specialized types, JSON, full-text and spatial search, hierarchical data, temporal history, and portability decisions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Upsert and MERGE differences
items.text: Upsert and MERGE differences changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: Identity and generated-key differences
items.text: Identity and generated-key differences changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Transaction and DDL differences
items.text: Transaction and DDL differences is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, product_id
LIMIT 5;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query runs on the common SQL lab schema. For specialist lessons, compare the portable pattern with the engine-specific extension described in the lesson.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate cross-database sql compatibility using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic standard sql vs. dialect extensions and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Cross-Database SQL Compatibility is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
